# Copper April 2010 

- April started on a promising note in the wake of the re-emergence of investor risk appetite during the latter stages of March, with official 3-month prices rising by $129/t to $7971/t on the 6th, their highest level since the end of July 2008.  However, copper, along with most other markets was adversely affected by two events that occurred during the latter half of the month and these were responsible for wiping ~$500/t off 3m quotes over the balance of April.  On the 19th news broke that Goldman Sachs had been accused of fraud by US regulators, driving prices down by $258/t.  Subsequently on the 24th, Standard and Poors downgraded Greece’s debt rating to junk status, paring 3m copper by a further $240/t. 

- During Cesco Week one of the key topics of debate centred around copper prices and whether (or not) current levels were likely to be sustainable.  Most people that we spoke to were of the opinion that current quotes were out of kilter with the market’s fundamentals, although they found it extremely difficult to quantify what might be a more realistic and/or sustainable level.  In an attempt to address this question we have reverted to the time-honoured method of looking at history to see whether this can provide guidance for the future. 

- It has come to our attention that demand, outside of China, has been recovering at a much quicker pace than most (ourselves included) had originally anticipated.  Indeed, the consumers themselves were surprised at the strength of the recovery.  However, on the downside wire rod and brass mills manufacturers alike reported that the strong order levels reflected restocking rather than any significant pick up in end-use demand.  Thus, while order levels through Q2 are reported to be strong there is concern that this momentum may not be maintained from Q3 onwards. 

- Spot concentrate business activity remained relatively quiet during April with less than a handful of tenders (three in fact) on offer.  The headline TC/RCs for two of these sales were reportedly negative, implying the willingness on the part of the purchasers to pay prices in excess of LME quotes.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market De

velopments 

**Prices held firm during the first half of the month** April started on a promising note in the wake of the re-emergence of investor risk appetite during the latter stages of March, with official 3-month prices rising by $129/t to $7971/t on the 6th.  This was their highest level since the end of July 2008 when prices reached $8073/t.  While a downward correction ensued over the course of the next two days (official 3-month quotes fall to $7833/t on the 8th) this was short-lived and prices soon recovered and continued to trade above $7900/t for most of the period through to the 16th.  However, copper, along with most other markets was adversely affected by two events that occurred during the latter half of the month and these were responsible for wiping ~$500/t off 3m quotes over the balance of April.  On the 19th news broke that Goldman Sachs had been accused of fraud by US regulators, driving prices down by $258/t.  Subsequently on the 24th, Standard and Poors downgraded Greece’s debt rating to junk status, paring 3m copper by a further $240/t. Despite this second half sell off, as of the 29th April prices averaged $7851/t, i.e. up by 4.8% over March ($7494/t) and also the highest monthly average since July 2008. 

**Positive sentiment from annual CESCO gathering** During the first two weeks of the month prices were supported by positive sentiment that emanated from the industry’s annual CESCO gathering in Chile and from the release of encouraging economic data.  One of the main bullish factors cited during CESCO Week was the demand outlook in the developed world, with a number of consumers pointing to a stronger pace of recovery than was previously expected, despite construction activity remaining at low levels.  In addition, it became apparent that various mining companies were still not making their production targets on account of disruptions.  As an example, at the start of April an illegal strike began at the 160kt/a OK Tedi Mine in Papua New Guinea where workers were protesting over bonus payments. However, employees agreed to return to work on the 17th after an MOU agreement was signed.  The MOU committed all parties to resolve employee grievances by the 1st August this year.  Any matters unresolved by that time will be referred to an Independent Arbitrator for judgement. 

**Economic data releases continue to be positive** Also supporting official quotes during the first two weeks of the month was the release of positive economic data.  In the US, data for March showed an unexpected 162k rise in non farm payrolls, manufacturing activity reaching its highest level since July 2004 and signs of consumer spending picking up after car sales increased by 22% in March from a year earlier.  Manufacturing activity outside of the US also continued to recover; March Purchasing Managers Indices for Japan, the Eurozone and China remained firmly above 50, the level between expansion and contraction.  While these factors helped support

prices through to the 16th, further upward movement was capped by data which showed the pace of Chinese bank lending had slowed in March. **Risk aversion triggered** On the 19th the market was stunned by the announcement that America’s financial regulator, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), was to sue Goldman Sachs for allegedly defrauding investors through the creation and sale of collateralised debt obligations linked to subprime mortgages (an accusation that the company denies). As a consequence official 3-month quotes fell by $258/t (-3.2%) on the day to $7683/t. Sentiment was also dented by the introduction of fresh measures aimed at curbing growth in China’s property market which is in danger of overheating. Under the new regulations banks are unable to make loans for 3rd properties in cities where prices have increased sharply, or lend to people who are unable to provide proof of social security payments. The announcement of the new measures had a negative impact on sentiment because China’s buoyant construction sector has been a major support to copper demand growth over the past twelve months. #### **Copper LME open interest vs copper price** 300000 8000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - April 2010 Page 2 of 25 Copper Monthly Update Prices did recover, albeit briefly, between the 20th and 25th, but another bout of panic selling occurred on the 28th following Greece’s credit ranking being lowered to junk status. This saw official 3-month quotes settling at $7448.50/t on the day. Prices have since edged lower at the time of writing. **LME open interest suggests no build in bearish sentiment** Despite the weaker price environment, recent LME open interest data suggests that the copper market continues to be dominated by the longs, as has been the case for much of the past year. From March 25th, copper prices were pushed steeply higher by new long positions, reaching a 2010 peak on April 6th, just shy of the $8000/t mark. After flirting with that level for a time, prices came down, in tandem with profit taking on long positions. While long liquidation may well continue for a while yet, especially given events in Greece, open interest data does not yet suggest any wholesale increase in bearish sentiment building in copper. **Exchange stocks increase** Total exchange stocks increased during the month with a large net increase in SHFE inventories outweighing a net drop in LME stocks. Comex inventories were unchanged at 91.7kt. As of the 29th, exchange inventories rose by a net 20.8kt to 780.5kt. This represented their highest level since December 2003 and was the equivalent of 15.6 days of co

nsumption. As noted, the rise reflected SHFE inventories increasing by a net 34kt to 189.4kt, their highest level since August 2002. The rise partly reflected heightened scrap receipts as well as reduced spot business resulting from the combination of high copper prices and tighter credit availability. Meanwhile on the LME, inventories fell by a net 13.1kt to 499.3kt; their lowest level thus far this year. The decline was expected in light of cancelled warrants totalling 17kt at the end of last month. The largest withdrawals in LME warrants this month occurred in Europe where inventories fell by a net 5.9kt to 65.4kt with steady deliveries out of warehouses located in Liverpool (- 2.5kt) and Bilbao (-2.5kt). At the time of writing (the 29th), LME cancelled warrants totalled 26.4kt, suggesting that further withdrawals will take place in the coming weeks. We would also expect European inventories to continue declining in light of improving demand conditions (see Consumption). **European premia strengthen** European premia strengthened during the month, reflecting both improved demand conditions across the region and strong premia in China. European premia have risen in the wake of cathodes continuing to be diverted from this market to China in order to benefit from higher premia. Meanwhile demand for spot cathode rose earlier in the month when consumers looked to fix prices at elevated levels in fear of them moving higher amid a background of low stocks throughout the supply chain and restocking requirements at the start of the new quarter. Chilean and grade A cathode from Rotterdam thus rose from $70/t over LME in March to $80/t in April. Italian warrants continued to trade at a slightly higher premia of $85/t while standard grade cathode was unchanged at $20/t over LME due to relatively tight scrap supplies. **US premia supported by transport problems** US premia edged higher for the second consecutive month in April, increasing from 4-4.5c/lb at the end of March to 4-4.5c/lb in April. However, the firmer level reflected transport difficulties rather than any significant improvement in underlying demand. We understand that truck availability during the month has become tight due to competition (for the trucks) from the agricultural markets in the Gulf of Mexico. The transport companies tend to favour the agricultural markets because higher freight rates can be achieved. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

**Chinese premia weaken** Chinese premia weakened further during April, falling from $90-100/t in March to around $80/t presently. As was the

case in March, the lower level reflected reduced arbitrage opportunities with SHFE prices trading at a discount to LME quotes throughout April.  The sharp rise in SHFE inventories during the month also dampened premia.  According to traders, the Chinese market has become particularly quiet of late in terms of fresh buying interest.

Copper Monthly Update 

**The key topic of debate during Cesco Week centred around the price outlook** During Cesco Week one of the key topics of debate centred around copper prices and whether (or not) current levels were likely to be sustainable.  Most people that we spoke to were of the opinion that current quotes were out of kilter with market fundamentals, although they found it extremely difficult to quantify what might be a more realistic and/or sustainable level.  In an attempt to address this question we have reverted to the time-honoured method of looking at history to see whether this can provide guidance for the future.  As part of this exercise we have compared annual average cash copper prices in the context of marginal (i.e. ninth decile) cash production costs in nominal terms and have also added annual metal stocks expressed in days of consumption.  What the chart below shows is that in a well-supplied market (i.e. between 1998 to 1999 and 2001 to 2003) where metal stocks were above average levels the difference between cash prices and marginal costs was relatively minimal.  However, as one might expect, under tight market conditions when stocks are well below average levels there is far less correlation between prices and marginal costs with the former being driven upwards by pent up demand.  This was clearly evident during the period 1994 to 1997 and even more so between 2004 and 2008. Interestingly, the average copper price during Q1 2009 traded at $3435/t which was very close to the ninth decile of cash costs for that year.  The real disconnect has occurred since then with prices rising significantly in tandem with a large increase in metal stocks.  Today, the overall metal stock position is reminiscent of the market back in 1998/1999 i.e. at a time when prices were closely correlated to marginal costs.  However, current prices are approximately double the level of prevailing marginal costs which, to our mind, is an uncomfortably high differential on the basis of historical precedent. One might of course argue that copper costs are currently suppressed by high by-product prices but this does not appear to be the case at the marginal cost level under anything other than extreme price movements.  In the final analysis, current marginal costs are well below prices that would be necessary to incentivise sufficient project development and so we do not believe that a decline in prices to the marginal cost level is justifiable.  However, we do remain unconvinced of the sustainability of current price levels and our forecasts therefore t

ake account of what we notionally describe as an investment portfolio “bleed out” over the next year or so. #### **Copper Prices, Marginal Cash Costs and Stocks** Current Price

**Demand in H1 stronger than expected** Following several conversations with cathode consumers during the month it has come to our attention that demand, outside of China, has been recovering at a much quicker pace than most (ourselves included) had originally anticipated (see Consumption). Indeed, the consumers themselves were surprised at the strength of the recovery. However, on the downside wire rod and brass mills manufacturers alike reported that the strong order levels reflected restocking rather than any significant pick up in end-use demand. Thus, while order levels through Q2 are reported to be strong there is concern that this momentum may not be maintained from Q3 onwards. This was also reiterated by our Chinese sources who informed us that next month’s order books may not be as strong as those witnessed during the first four months of the year. Thus, while our overall annual demand forecast for 2010 is little changed from last month, we have revised our quarterly estimates to reflect the stronger demand conditions in H1. We now estimate that there was a global market surplus of ~350kt in Q1 compared with ~420kt previously. In Q2 we have increased our market deficit from 182kt to ~240kt. For the year as a whole we forecast that supply will exceed demand by ~180kt and average prices will increase by 38.5% year on year to $7160/t ($3.25/lb). **Full demand recovery expected in 2011** In 2011 global refined consumption is forecast to increase by 6.5%, to ~19.4Mt, as a full recovery outside of China takes place. At the same time refined production is expected to grow by 5.8%, to ~19.5Mt, which will result in an essentially balanced market. Metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, will fall from 75 days to 72 days. Despite the improving market conditions we are forecasting a modest fall in prices to an average of $6825/t ($3.10/lb) for the reasons described above. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - April 2010 Page 5 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Technical Analysis Copper repeatedly challenged resistance at $8,000/t over early April but failed to break through on a closing basis. Prices have subsequently pulled back to close at $7,415/t on the 28th . Over the next three months we are inclined to believe prices will try and move up with $9,000/t targeted on a break through $8,000/t. This said wider market malaise relating to the Euro could sufficiently dampen wider market sentiment to allow prices to fall to support around $7,100/t before further upward moves resume. Resistance is expected at $7,580-7,600/t (March 3rd high) and $8,000/t, close to the April highs. On the downside support is anticipated around $7,300/t, $7,100/t and at $6,900/t. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - April 2010 Page 6 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments The Chinese property sector has been causing concerns for the markets recently. Real estate prices rose sharply in March, up by 11.7% year on year, and new policy measures by the government have led to fears of a repeat of late 2007, where excessive policy measures in

troduced in an attempt to cool the market led to a collapse in construction activity. With construction activity in China having such a strong economic multiplier with heavy industry and the wider economy, it is important for policy makers to get it right. There are good reasons to believe that we will not see a repeat of 2007 in the real estate market, and indeed that construction activity in China will continue to grow robustly through 2010. The development of property price growth in China needs to be put into context. Firstly, the 11.7% gain in March (which is likely an underestimate – other indices estimate growth closer to 20%) is partly a base effect, as property prices were weak in early 2009. Secondly, unlike in 2007, the rise in prices has not been seen across all property types. Luxury residential prices have rocketed, particularly in teir-1 coastal cities, and to a lesser extent so have commercial property prices. Low-end residential prices, on the other hand, only increase by ~2% year on year in March, and given that urbanisation is concentrated at the lower end of the market, this distinction is important (total residential accounts for ~78% of construction activity in China). #### **Income had been growing faster than house prices until now** 16% Real estate price growth

The other important factor for contextualizing price rises is affordability. 2010 is the first time in the past decade in which property prices have been growing faster than urban wages (on a year-on-year basis), meaning that by historical standards affordability is still good. Affordability is likely to improve through 2010, as wage inflation picks up and government measures to curb property speculation kick in. In addition, affordability is much greater outside of the tier-1 coastal cities, where urbanisation is expected to concentrated. So what has been the official response to the rise in property prices? The government has taken the threat of a real estate bubble seriously, implementing a number of measures to curtail speculation in the housing market. Earlier in April, the required down payment for second homes was raised to 50% and mortgage rates for second homes were effectively increased from 4.2% to 6.5%. The minimum holding period of a property for a 5.5% tax exemption on property sales has been extended from two to five years. Tight mortgage restrictions will also be enforced for property investors, and real estate developers are now required to submit their fund-raising plans to the central government for approval. Furthermore, a property tax is being discussed in case price appreciation in property becomes rampant. But perhaps most importantly, there have been no proposals to drastically

limit lending to property developers, as occurred in 2007, which could have brought construction activity to a rapid slowdown/ halt. As well as acting to curb speculation, there have also been measures to increase the supply of affordable housing. The Ministry of Land and Resources will make 1800 square kilometres of land available for residential construction in 2010, a 135% increase over 2009. This is roughly one and a half times the size of the whole of Hong Kong. 77% of the land will be restricted to public housing or units under 90 square meters. Of course, there are no guarantees that all the land made available will be used, but it should help to ensure that robust growth in construction activity, as we have seen in the first quarter, will continue through the duration of 2010. Floor space under construction in Q1 has risen by 36% from a year earlier and by over 50% from the first quarter of 2008. **So urce: N B S** In the USA, there have been some modestly encouraging signs in construction activity, but little to get excited about. Housing starts rose by 1.6% month on month to an annualised rate of 626,000 units, the highest rate since November 2008, although still down by 72% from the peak of activity in January 2006. The US residential construction market still faces strong headwinds in 2010, with the first-time homebuyer tax credit expiring on April 30th , and a glut of foreclosed properties still expected to come onto the market through the year, limiting demand for new properties. If first housing starts continued at their Q1 pace over the rest of the year, 2010 would see housing starts rise by 11.5% on an annual basis. On the non-residential side of things, the American Institute of Architects billing index suggests that construction activity will continue to fall through the course of 2010, and construction spending on office and commercial space looks especially weak. The European construction market is also expected to have a tough year ahead. The March euro zone construction PMI reported housing and commercial activity numbers of 38.8 and 41.4 respectively, well below the 50 threshold between expansion and contraction. Coming in at 40, the new orders component was also in contraction territory, suggesting that activity will continue to contract in the coming months. A further blow to developers in Europe is that input material prices are rising at their fastest rate since the third quarter of 2008. #### **Euro zone construction PMIs** 65

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - April 2010 Page 8 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Consumption **Final numbers for 2009 continue to be reported** We have made a series of revisions to our 2009 demand estimates since our last monthly report to reflect official reported numbers for last year. The reported data showed that demand in Europe during Q4 last year was stronger than we had originally anticipated, particularly in Germany, which resulted in us lifting our European demand figure by a net 48kt to ~2.7Mt. However, this gain was offset by the downturn in demand in North America during the latter stages of last year being much steeper than previously expected. We also lowered our 2009 demand estimates for Australia, India, Mexico and Poland. Thus we now estimate that global refined copper consumption decreased by 3.9% last year to just over 17.2Mt. For this year and next we forecast that demand will recover by 5.7% and 6.5% to ~18.2Mt and 19.4Mt respectively. ### **USA** **Surprising improvement in US wire rod demand** Some wire rod producers in the US have reported a small pick up in orders in recent weeks. While it is typical for demand to be stronger at this time of year, because of the better weather leading to increased construction activity, producers have been surprised by the strength of the recovery. According to our sources some sectors are performing better than others. The market for magnet wire is doing reasonably well as are orders for wire and cable consumed within the renewable energy sector i.e solar energy and wind production. Elsewhere, the telecoms market is stronger than expected while demand for building wire remains dampened. This is not surprising in light of the parlous state of the US construction sector. Latest government statistics showed that housing starts increased by 1.6% in March from a month earlier. However, at 626k units (annualised) they were down by 20.2% from March last year and by over 70% from the peak back in 2006. **Restocking responsible for the stronger than expected recovery** One wire rod producer we spoke to believed that the stronger than expected rise in orders reflected restocking rather than any significant recovery in demand from the end-use markets. Inventories throughout the supply chain were drawn down to a minimum last year and consumers of copper wire rod are now concerned that should there be a sudden recovery in demand for their end use products, against an improving economic outlook, they will not be able to respond sufficiently. **Wire rod capacity below par** Despite the stronger than expected recovery in orders, many wire rod mills are reportedly operating below 50%. However, this does not apply to Southwire’s Carollton plant which is running above this. According to the company t

his is largely due to the company’s recent acquisition of American Insulated Wire (AIW). It is hoped that the acquisition of the AIW assets will allow Southwire to become stronger in the construction, industrial, OEM and retail market segments. As a consequence of its recent acquisitions Southwire is now expecting a small increase in its production this year. At the end of last year the company was forecasting a decline of between 1-2% in 2010. **US demand for copper and copper alloy products picked up** Demand for copper and copper alloy products has also picked up in the US where orders in Q1 were much stronger than expected, according to our sources. However, brass mills are yet to be convinced that the pick up reflects the start of a sustainable recovery. One copper semis producer reported that following conversations with his customers the improvement in orders reflected re-stocking rather than any significant recovery in underlying demand from the end-use markets. Likewise with the wire rod market, the pipeline between the semis producers and the end-user is very lean. Thus consumers along the supply chain are ordering extra material in order to build up their stocks in readiness for any sustainable recovery in demand. **Mixed demand from the different market sectors** Demand for copper and copper alloy products from the different market sectors was mixed during Q1. According

to our sources orders from the industrial sector performed well as did orders from the auto sector.  This was reflected in the production of car and light vehicles (LV) which increased by 62% year on year in Q1 to 1.9M units.  Output in March was 52.6% higher than a year ago at 726k units.  On an annualised basis this equated to 8.7M units which represented a return to 2008 output levels.  The increase reflected fresh underlying demand for autos as well AS inventory build (of autos).  Elsewhere demand from the construction sector remained extremely weak. 

**Positive order levels reported for Q2** Brass mills have continued to report firm order levels during this quarter with some copper semi producers reporting sales above budget.  They also confirmed that their customers further downstream are also reporting healthy order levels.  However, there is concern that this upward momentum will not be carried through into Q3 as the restocking process slows down.  With this in mind we do not expect a full recovery in US refined copper demand to take place this year.  Thus we forecast that US refined copper consumption will increase by 2.5% in 2010 to just below 1.6Mt.  While this may seem like a healthy rate of recovery it equates to a gain of just 38kt. However, in 2011 a much stronger recovery is anticipated where demand is forecast to increase by 4.3% to just over 1.6Mt. 

### **Africa** 

**North African wire rod production continues to perform well** Demand for copper wire rod in Egypt continues to perform well where production at some plants is expected to equal last year’s high levels.  Results from our copper wire rod survey showed that the production of Egyptian copper wire rod increased by 9.7% last year to just under 140kt.  The increase was supported by healthy demand from both the domestic and overseas markets.  According to latest data from the World Bureau of Metal Statistics exports last year totalled 4.7kt.  This was up 29.1% from a year earlier and represented their highest level ever.  Egypt’s main export markets are Europe, the Middle East and Africa.  However, one major wire rod producer reported that they are not exporting much to Europe presently because demand has not been that strong.  Therefore any demand in Europe has been fulfilled by European producers because they have been able to offer a much more competitive price due to lower freight costs.  Demand for copper wire rod from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is also weak.  This mainly reflects poor wire and cable orders from the construction sector in Dubai.  In contrast copper wire rod demand in Saudia Arabia is reported to be strong, reflecting healthy growth within the construction sector.  However, Egyptian wire rod producers are unable to benefit from this healthy demand because orders are being met from domestic production which has been growing steadily since 2008.  According to our sources Saudia Arabia’s wire rod producers are currently running close to capacity (~

230kt).  Taking the above into account we forecast that Egyptian refined copper consumption will increase by 4.9% this year to 215kt. 

### **Europe** 

**Europe’s construction sector is still contracting** Although Europe’s manufacturing sector is showing some signs of life the construction sector is not.  Bad weather in January and February meant that the sector got off to a bad start with construction output in the first quarter of 2010 falling by over 8% year on year which marked the seventh consecutive quarter of decline.  The region’s housing sector remained the weakest segment with the housing component of the eurozone construction purchasing manager’s index climbing to just 38.9 in March. 

**Improving wire rod orders** Despite the poor performing construction sector demand for copper wire rod in some areas has been improving at a quicker pace than previously anticipated.  One producer reported that his sales levels are now back to more normal levels.  Orders from the automotive and power sectors are reportedly doing very well.  However, while encouraging the same producer did warn that there was little evidence to suggest that the recovery in orders reflected any significant improvement in end-use demand.  He believed the pick up reflected his customers restocking due to lean pipeline supplies.  Also, the improvement in wire rod demand has not been universal across the region where some wire rod plants in Italy and Spain continue to struggle.  Indeed one plant is believed to be running sporadically.

**CESCO Week discussions focus on China’s growing market influence and potential smelter casualties** During CESCO Week many of our discussions with concentrate producers and consumers focused on China’s growing influence in this market as well as who, and when might there be the long-anticipated smelter casualties, given the chronic overcapacity in this sector of the market.  One conclusion was that, setting aside the relative economics of each plant, the most logical smelter closures should occur in countries that lack sufficient domestic mine feed and where refined output exceeds local demand by a considerable amount.  Countries that fit these criteria include Bulgaria, Canada, Finland, Japan, Philippines and Sweden.  That said Bulgaria should be viewed in the context of it having a wider, regional market both for concentrates feed and metals sales.  Also, developments in Canada during 2010 will see the closure of 230kt of smelting capacity by mid year (Flin Flon and Kidd Creek).  In addition, Pasar, the only smelter in the Philippines is majority owned by the world’s second largest copper concentrate trader and Boliden will soon have more domestic concentrate feed from its expanded Aitik mine and it plans to expand the electronic scrap re

cycling capacity at the Ronnskar plant in Sweden by 167%. Many people that we spoke to in Santiago agreed that the next round of closures could see the loss of two smelters in Japan and one in Europe, accounting for perhaps 700kt/a of annual capacity. As we have mentioned previously, the medium-term shortfall in concentrate supplies relative to the optimal global primary smelter utilisation rate (88%) is ~1.5Mt/a Cu and so the loss of three plants would amount to almost 50% of this gap. However, there can be no guarantee that this medium-term supply gap will remain static. We estimate that on the basis of projected smelter capacity growth and utilisation rates, China’s cathode import requirements will be around 2.6Mt/a for the next three years and this will no doubt tempt existing and potential new entrants into constructing additional smelting capacity in order to raise the levels of value-added copper production domestically. #### **Long-Term TC/RCs (excluding PP in constant 2010$)** 45 Growing China Effect

**Concerns also raised about the eventual impact of China’s concentrate market dominance** While some of the CESCO participants were not really fazed by China’s growing dominance in the custom concentrates market, a number of people felt that the eventual outcome of this could be exceedingly detrimental to concentrate sellers. These concerns stem from a view that China is prepared to accept artificially low TC/RCs today in order to drive out competition, but as the future dominant force in the industry China could in time dictate or at least heavily influence future contractual arrangements. As an example, Chinese smelters could insist upon lower metal accountability, the reintroduction of price participation, higher precious metals refining charges, later payment terms and even TC/RCs expressed in RMB instead of US dollars and a pricing structure linked to the SHFE market as opposed to the LME. Of course, such an outcome assumes that the large concentrate suppliers will simply roll over and agree to these changes. In reality, mines will sell their output into the custom concentrate market so long as the economics of doing so merit this (as is the case at present). The alternative to this strategy is to build or acquire integrated smelting capacity if market conditions warrant. ## Blister/anode and scrap markets **No. 2 scrap spreads widen on lower demand** US scrap dealers have reported a further widening of scrap spreads in the US during April. ## Production news 

**Mine disruptions still remain very much in the spotlight** Various mining companies have reported their Q1 production results over the past month and it is clear that disruptions remain very much in the spotlight.  Extraordinary rains in Andalucнa delayed pit operations at Inmet’s Las Cruces project for one month while a 15-day plant shutdown for modifications further hampered copper output.  In addition, the company is awaiting permits that will allow it to ship direct smelting ores from the mine site from next month but in the meantime Inmet has reduced its 2010 output guidance for Las Luces from 55kt SxEw Cu to 36kt and from 18kt Cu in ore sales to 12kt Cu.  Elsewhere, an illegal strike at Inmet’s 18%-owned Ok Tedi mine in PNG at the start of April was called off on the 17<sup>th</sup> .  The company estimates that lost production amounted to 5kt Cu but essential maintenance previously planned for later in the year was carried out during this down time which should enable the operation to recoup some of the lost output.  In other news, industrial action at the 18kt/a Cobriza mine in Peru that started on March 23<sup>rd</sup> was called off on April 5<sup>th</sup> .  We also he

ar that there has been no tangible progress in the long-standing strikes at Vale Inco’s Sudbury and Voisey’s Bay operations while unions at Lundin Mining’s 90kt/a Neves Corvo mine have called for industrial action from May 5<sup>th</sup> to May 12<sup>th</sup> .  In terms of other disruptions the restart of the Cananea mine in Mexico appears to be edging towards later rather than sooner with striking miners refusing to leave the mine site despite having lost their legal challenge and they have even threatened to blow up the facility if faced with forceful removal.  In addition, the full effects of the major Chilean earthquake and numerous aftershocks on the country’s copper output won’t be fully known for another month or so, although the latest data from the INE shows that Chilean production in March 2010 was 451kt Cu, i.e. up by 5% year on year and by 14% month on month thanks to strong results from Collahuasi, El Tesoro, Codelco Norte and Salvador.  Offsetting these gains were lower output at all of Codelco’s other divisions, at Escondida SxEw due to safety intervention in the electrowinning plant, at Candelaria due to SAG mill and conveyor problems and also at Anglo American Norte, Cerro Colorado, Michilla and Spence.

**Uzbek Government invests in Almalyk mine expansions** Various initiatives are under way in Uzbekistan to bolster copper production at the state-owned Almalyk complex.  Refined output has fallen from an historical peak of 140kt/a to 70-80kt currently.  The first initiative involves expanding the Kalmakir mine, the main source of copper concentrates for Almalyk.  The modernisation of the open pit mine/mill will increase the mine's output by 3.5Mt/a from 27Mt/a at an estimated capital cost of $98.7M. The Uzbek Government will also invest $23.5m in the Sary-Cheku mine to raise ore throughput capacity by 1Mt/a, to 5Mt/a by 2015.  The modernisation will begin before the end of H1 2010. The project includes the purchase of additional mining and transport equipment and renovation of the railroad which connects the mine to the mill.  Finance will be provided through loans from Uzbek banks.  The Sary-Cheku m

ine has been in service since 1974 and its maximum capacity reached 4Mt/a of ore, however, due to the gradual deterioration of equipment, the mine's output has decreased to 2Mt/a in recent years.  At an ore throughput rate of 5Mt/a the mine’s contribution to copper-in-concentrate production should be ~15kt/a.  Another small mine, Khandiza, is to be commissioned in mid 2010 and should provide the Almalyk complex with a further 4-5kt/a of copper. 

**Japanese smelters announce H1 2010 smelter production plans** Japanese copper smelters have recently released their production plans for the six-month period from April to September 2010. **KCM mid-shaft loading facility commissioned at the Konkola Deep Project** On April 20<sup>th</sup> KCM officially commissioned the mid-shaft loading facility at the No.4 shaft within its Konkola Deep project. **Nippon Mining to extend smelter shutdown intervals at Saganoseki and Tamano** Nippon Mining plans to change the shutdown intervals at its Saganoseki and Tamano copper smelter furnaces from one year to as much as six years. Initially, maintenance inspections will occur every two years to check the results of the new system.  Currently

, approximately 30% of the heat-proof bricks are replaced each year at both smelters at a cost of approximately $20M. However, the longer shutdown intervals are not intended to raise production but rather to reduce the furnace burden by lowering the operating rate. For Saganoseki this will result in a decline in raw material charge from 210t/hr to 180t/hr and this may also improve recoveries because the extended residence time of the copper within the furnace.
